Tap **Keep** \- one tap, seconds. Leave it unkept and it expires after 30 days. And **minus the part you quit** means far less of the filing, not none: you skim what it filed and tap to keep - one tap, seconds, the only chore left. Then it stays useful because you never have to re-file it.

You don’t start at a blank canvas with a brave little "New Note" button, either. Drag in the folder of 30 PDFs a past tool promised to read and didn’t. Text-layer PDFs read fine today - title, authors, abstract, body - as a first pass you correct in a glance; scans and image-only pages don’t parse yet, and it’s honest about which is which. Because it’s your literature, nothing changes behind your back: every change is logged with a plain-language before-and-after, attributed, and one tap to put back. You stay the **editor of record**.

Your paste is processed by an AI to build the map; unkept trial spaces expire after 30 days. Your space is private to you; the AI acts as you and sees only what you can. Where your data lives - including the honest answer for pre-publication material - is at /docs.

Who this is for

> You loved the connected-map idea and got tired of being the librarian of your own field.

If hand-building your slip-box is the thinking for you - if drawing every link by hand is the part you love - Naumu takes that job away and you’ll miss it. And if you want offline-first, local Markdown files you own forever with a deep plugin ecosystem, that’s Obsidian, and it’s genuinely good at it. One hard line up front: your paste is processed on a server to build the map, and your private space lives online once you Keep it - if your unpublished data can never touch a server you don’t control, check /docs first.

Naumu is for the other researcher. The one with a folder of 30 abstracts, a Zotero library you’re scared to open, and three reference systems you’ve already abandoned - who wants the map built and kept without becoming its full-time gardener.

Why it holds up

## A Zettelkasten without the second job.

### It draws the links, not just stores them

The slip-box dream only worked if you drew every backlink by hand, forever - and the week you fell behind it quietly died. Naumu infers the connections from plain text and draws them: no \[\[brackets\]\], no nightly grooming, no manual re-linking.

### Every fact traces to its source

Ask in plain language and the answer comes back with the note or abstract it was pulled from and a one-click path back - the line in your note, the place in the PDF you dragged in. Nothing floats free of where you read it.

### It lasts because you never re-file it

No tag system to design first, no folders to reorganize - there were never folders. You correct a handful of first-pass links instead of grooming a vault, and it doesn’t decay the week you get busy the way a hand-linked one does.

FAQ

## The stuff you’re actually wondering.

Can it read my actual PDFs?

Can I cite from this? How reliable is the trace?

Do I have to sign up or set anything up to try it?

Am I in control, or is the AI?

Can my AI assistant read and write my literature too?

## Drop your pile.

Throw in an abstract, a margin note, or the whole folder of PDFs, and watch it build into a connected map you can finally just ask. No signup, no email - and one tap to Keep it when it earns it.

## Scope of what I'm building

The goal is a self-organizing knowledge system: a chat-first interface where any input (text, pasted content, dragged files, links) is automatically parsed, converted into structured graph data (nodes and edges), and made queryable in natural language, without the user manually filing, tagging, or linking anything.

## Core data model

The system stores information as a property graph. Each **node** represents a discrete real-world entity or concept (a person, client, meeting, task, document, claim, or note). Each **node** has a type drawn from a user- or system-defined schema, a set of typed attributes, a creation timestamp, and a provenance reference pointing back to the exact source text/file/message it was extracted from. **Edges** connect nodes and represent typed relationships (e.g., "owns," "attended," "relates to," "responds to"), each edge also carrying a timestamp and provenance reference. The schema (allowed node types, attribute definitions, edge types) must be user-configurable but auto-inferred by default from ingested content.

## Ingestion pipeline

Build an ingestion pipeline accepting arbitrary unstructured input: typed/pasted text, dragged files (Markdown, PDF with a text layer, images, audio memos), links, and bulk exports/folders. For each input, run entity/claim extraction to identify candidate nodes and attributes, run relation extraction to identify candidate edges linking new content to existing graph nodes by semantic similarity (not manual linking), and store an explicit low-confidence flag on any inferred link so it can be surfaced for user confirmation. For bulk imports (e.g., a folder of existing notes or a vault export), run this pipeline in batch and produce a review summary showing what was parsed cleanly versus what needs manual correction — do not silently guess on ambiguous content.

## Query engine

Implement a natural-language query interface over the graph: user asks a question in plain language, the system translates it into a structured graph query (traversal/filter across node types, attributes, and edges), executes it, and returns an answer that cites the specific source node(s), including original text snippet, timestamp, and file/message provenance for every fact used. No answer may be returned without a traceable source link.

## Views and structured surfaces

On top of the raw graph, build saved "views" — filtered, sorted, grouped projections of nodes (e.g., all clients with open renewals, grouped by owner) that behave like dynamic tables/lists, auto-updating as the underlying graph changes. These views are how the system replaces dedicated CRM/tracker interfaces without maintaining separate databases.

## Multi-tenant spaces and access control

Implement isolated "spaces" (workspace containers) each holding their own graph, with membership and per-space or per-node visibility rules (roles: owner, member, viewer). Support inviting members, assigning roles, and restricting which parts of a graph are visible to whom.

## Agent/AI participant layer

Design AI "agents" as first-class graph participants with the same read/write permissions and audit trail as human users — every write an agent makes must be logged, attributed to that agent identity, diffable (plain-language before/after), and revertible in one action. Support: (a) hosted agents that run scheduled tasks against the graph (e.g., periodic summarization or reconciliation), and (b) external/BYO agent runtimes that authenticate via issued credentials and act as a space member through a protocol interface (e.g., MCP-style tool exposure of graph read/write/query operations).

## External integrations

Build connector modules for common external tools (chat platforms, issue trackers, document tools) that one-way or two-way sync external items (messages, tickets, docs) into the graph as nodes with correct typing and provenance, running as background sync jobs so the graph updates without requiring the user to migrate data up front. Also implement inbound webhooks: a per-integration signed endpoint that accepts external events and triggers an agent action inside the relevant space.

## Export and data ownership

Implement full graph export (all nodes, edges, attributes, provenance) in a portable structured format (e.g., JSON) so users can extract their complete dataset at any time.

## Trial/session lifecycle

Support anonymous, no-signup trial sessions where a space is created immediately on first input, exists in full working form, and automatically expires (e.g., after 30 days) unless the user takes an explicit action to persist/claim it permanently under an account.
